The evening study hall at the residential school in Dehradun had a rule: no talking after seven. But Disha could feel the silence around her had changed since the pre-board results went up. She had come first. Naveen, who used to share her table and his tiffin, now sat three tables away.

On Tuesday she heard two girls in the corridor. "She'll only help if you beg." It stung.

Disha thought about scoring lower next time just to have people back. Then she thought about how hard she'd worked for this and how much she still wanted it. No.

She didn't pin her marks up or talk about them. After study hall, she photocopied her organic chemistry notes at the office and left a set on each table in her row, including Naveen's, with a slip: "In case these help. Ask me anything."

Naveen didn't come back to her table. But on Thursday, he asked Disha a question about reaction mechanisms, and Disha answered it slowly and carefully.

Sonali saw the number before she saw anything else: 29 out of 80 in the chemistry pre-board. She walked home through the market without noticing the crowds.

In her room she whispered, "Useless. Papa told everyone at the office I'd get ninety." She pictured his face, then her grandmother's. She felt she had brought shame on the whole house.

Her younger brother Yash knocked. "Didi? Dinner." Then, seeing her face, "It's just one paper, na?"

She almost snapped at him. Instead she sat with it. One paper. Not her. She took a sheet and wrote what had gone wrong: skipped two chapters of organic, panicked on the numericals, ran out of time on the last section.

Seeing it on paper, it looked less like a verdict and more like a to-do list.

The next morning she waited outside the staffroom for Mrs Gill. "Ma'am, I got 29. Can you help me make a recovery plan for the boards?" Mrs Gill pulled out a chair for her.

qa.a: Sonali got 29 out of 80.

"Uday, stay back a minute," Sharmila ma'am said as the bell rang.

He waited by her desk, eyes on the floor.

"Forty-one in the pre-board. You've never been below seventy. What happened?"

"I don't know, ma'am. I'm just stupid, I think." His voice cracked. "My father will say I've shamed the family. My whole family's watching this year."

"Look at me." She waited until he did. "You wrote a bad paper. That's not the same as being a bad student, or a bad son. Can you tell me three things that went wrong?"

He thought. "I didn't finish the syllabus. I didn't do any timed practice. And I froze on section C."

"Good. That's three things we can fix. Not a verdict." She pulled a planner from her drawer. "Two practice papers a week, timed, and you come to me on Thursdays for section C."

Uday wiped his eyes. "Thank you, ma'am."

"And Uday? Asking me was the right thing."
